lesson_title: Half a Doubling: Rational Exponents and Surds
hook_text: Money that doubles in a year — what does it do in half a year? That answer invents the fraction exponent.
clip_script: Money that doubles in a year. After one year, times two. After two years, two squared. The exponent is just how many doublings happened. Now the question that breaks the whole thing open: what happens in HALF a year? Whatever that factor is, doing it twice must give one full doubling. So it's the number whose square is two — the square root of two. And we write it two to the power one half. That's all a fraction exponent is. The bottom says how many equal steps make one whole multiplication. The top says how many steps you take. Sixteen to the power three quarters? Bottom is four — chop sixteen into four equal steps, that's the fourth root, which is two. Top is three — take three steps: two times two times two. Eight. And a minus sign in the exponent? That's stepping backwards, so you flip it. Twenty-seven to the minus two thirds: cube root of twenty-seven is three, squared is nine, flipped is one ninth. Never negative. Just upside down. Bottom is the root. Top is the power. Say it until it's automatic.
visual_style: A stokvel savings book filling up: coins doubling in stacks, one stack splitting into two equal half-year steps, a sixteen-block chopping into four, then three steps lighting up; a fraction flipping over for the negative exponent.
mood: Bright, practical, a small penny-drop moment.
pacing: Steady on the doubling, a beat of silence on the half-year question, brisk through the worked steps.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and turn every root sign into a power you can actually use.
